title: A Benedictine day at home
hook: a bell, a psalm, work, reading, a meal, silence

segments.voice: Yesterday, oblates: laypeople tied to one monastery, carrying the Rule into ordinary life. Your line was the rule at home. What piece of it made it through your front door? Day one thousand two hundred seven.

Six things. A bell. A psalm. Work. Reading. A meal. Silence. That's the whole list, and it's almost too plain to write down. But lay those six out across a day and something happens to the day. It stops being one long smear of tasks and screens and becomes a set of rooms, each with a door. For these past weeks this path has walked through Benedict's Rule, chapter by chapter. Today, the last day with Benedict, the question is simple: what does it look like when it's all put together, in a house that isn't a monastery? Today: a Benedictine day at home.
screen: `A BELL, A PSALM, WORK.` → `READING, A MEAL, SILENCE.` → `A DAY WITH DOORS.`

segments.voice: Start with the bell. In the Rule, the bell isn't a nag. It's a signal that the next thing has come, and at the signal for prayer, Benedict says, monks put down whatever is in their hands and go, nothing before the work of God. At home the bell might be an alarm, or the kettle, or a church bell down the street. Then the psalm. The monks pray at set hours, from the night office to the last prayer before sleep. At home it may be one psalm, morning or evening. Then work. Idleness, Benedict writes, is the enemy of the soul, so there are hours for work with the hands, and the tools are handled like the vessels of the altar. Then reading: hours set aside for slow, attentive reading of Scripture. Then a meal, eaten with others while someone reads aloud, with a measure of food and drink that's enough and not too much. Then silence, especially after the last prayer at night. Here's the thread that runs through every piece: balance. Benedict keeps asking for measure. When he describes the abbot, he asks him to arrange everything so that the strong have something to strive for and the weak have nothing to run from. Prayer doesn't swallow work. Work doesn't swallow reading. Nobody fasts to collapse, and nobody eats till they can't move. Benedict's word for this good judgment, in chapter sixty-four, is discretion, and he calls it the mother of virtues. So the Benedictine day isn't impressive. It's proportioned. Next comes a different house entirely. Tomorrow the path leaves the monastery and walks out on the road with Francis of Assisi.
screen: `THE BELL: THE NEXT THING HAS COME.` · `PSALM, WORK, READING, MEAL, SILENCE.` · `SOMETHING FOR THE STRONG, NOTHING TO FLEE.` · then, large: `DISCRETION, THE MOTHER OF VIRTUES.` · then: `NOT IMPRESSIVE. PROPORTIONED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: try one Benedictine hour. Settle, and breathe. Look at the rest of your day and choose one hour you could shape. Maybe a few minutes of a psalm, then work with no phone in reach, then a short stretch of reading, then a meal eaten slowly. Now practice the first piece: the bell. When this session's bell rings, treat it the way the Rule does: as the signal that the next thing has come. Until then, rest in the silence that ends a Benedictine day. The bell holds the time.
A Benedictine day at home. Bell, psalm, work, reading, meal and silence, kept in balance, the way the Rule shapes a monk's hours, brought into an ordinary house. Today's word.
screen: `A BENEDICTINE DAY AT HOME — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: balance. Today, if one thing has swallowed your day, give one other thing back its hour. Day one thousand two hundred seven.

howItsDone: Some Benedictine oblates and other laypeople shape their day around short times of the Liturgy of the Hours, a period of lectio divina, focused work and shared meals, adapted to family and job.

fork.setup: you're the abbot. some brothers are strong and eager, some are tired and frail. how do you set the demands of the day?
options: set them high, so only the strong stay.
set them low, so nobody is ever stretched.
arrange them so the strong have something to strive for and the weak nothing to run from.
fork.reveal: chapter sixty-four asks the abbot for exactly this, and calls the good judgment behind it discretion, the mother of virtues.

original.note: Latin: discretion, good judgment, which Benedict calls the mother of virtues in chapter sixty-four.

trapdoor: what you thought: a monastic day is grim and extreme.
what it means: bell, psalm, work, reading, meal and silence, held in balance so no one thing swallows the rest.
what a scholar hears: discretio, 'the mother of virtues' in chapter sixty-four, governs the whole Rule's measure.
